docs.title: Electrodes
docs.text: Connect surface electrodes for EEG or EMG. Both use the same front end: the ADS1299 is a general biopotential converter, and the difference between an EEG and an EMG setup is gain, sample rate and montage, which you set from the PC.

docs.title: A DAC or signal generator
docs.text: Drive the analog inputs with a known signal to check the whole chain, from amplifier to result. The board also has an internal test signal and a shorted-input mode for measuring its own noise.

docs.title: Simulated data from your PC
docs.text: Stream recorded or synthetic data from the PC straight into the board's processing, with no electrodes connected. Useful for developing an algorithm, or for measuring a model's accuracy on a known dataset.

docs.title: What runs on the board
docs.text: The processor has two cores. One handles acquisition and the links to the PC; the other runs the processing. A slow or busy algorithm cannot delay sampling, and the board reports dropped and missed samples at all times, so you can check that it didn't. How it works has the details.

docs.title: Signal chain
docs.text: Filtering, notch, DC removal, envelopes and band power run on the board in real time, next to acquisition. The reference app streams a 2–28 Hz filtered signal with a 50 Hz notch, and alpha, SSVEP and neurofeedback measures ten times a second.

docs.title: Edge ML
docs.text: Trained models run on the board and send their classifications to the PC with the data. An EEGNet model ported to the board reproduced the accuracy of its reference implementation.

docs.title: Researchers
docs.text: Run recordings from a desktop app: choose a preset, check the board with its built-in tests, and record. Every run saves the raw data, the board's health, and the settings it was recorded with.

docs.title: Developers
docs.text: Write your own processing as an app on the board, in C/C++, against one documented interface. Test it on simulated data from the PC, then run it on live signals without changing the recording side.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: ν-Φ is developed at the NeuRonICS Lab, IISc. Features described here are tested on the hardware; planned work is on the roadmap. Documentation and the developer kit are available to approved users. Request access.

docs.title: How ν-Φ works
docs.text: ν-Φ is a 32-channel biosignal acquisition board for EEG and EMG. It runs on a dual-core processor. Most boards share both cores between everything they do. ν-Φ gives each core one job, and draws a hard line between them.

docs.title: Where the signal comes from
docs.text:
The board's inputs can be driven in three ways:

  • Electrodes. Surface electrodes for EEG or EMG, connected to the analog front end.
  • A DAC or signal generator. A known analog signal on the same inputs, to test the whole chain from amplifier to result.
  • The PC. Recorded or synthetic data streamed over Wi-Fi or USB straight into the processing core, with the analog front end bypassed.

The front end is four ADS1299 converters, 8 channels each. The ADS1299 is a general biopotential converter, so EEG and EMG use the same hardware; the difference is the gain, sample rate and montage, which are all settings.

docs.title: Core 0: acquisition
docs.text:
The first core belongs to the board. It reads the four converters, gives every sample a sequence number and the current event marker, and publishes it exactly once. It also owns the links to the PC, over Wi-Fi or the USB cable, and sends everything that leaves the board in one ordered stream.

This core never waits for anything running on the other one. That is the rule the whole design is built around.

docs.title: Core 1: processing and edge ML
docs.text:
The second core runs apps. An app is a small program that:

  1. reads samples as they are published, at its own pace;
  2. processes them however it likes: filters, envelopes, windows, features, models;
  3. reports results, which the board sends to the PC alongside the data.

An app receives the raw signal from all 32 channels. The board applies no filtering of its own, so the processing is entirely the app's. Several apps can run at once, and each one sees every sample.

When the data comes from the PC instead of the converters, apps see it exactly as they would see live samples. That makes it possible to develop and test an algorithm before any recording.

docs.title: One contract between them
docs.text:
An app sees the board through a single header file: the contract. It holds a dozen functions, for reading samples, reading the current sample rate and gain, describing the app, and reporting results. Adding an app changes nothing in the board's code.

Apps report results in four shapes:

Shape What it carries Typical use Class a classification, up to 4 class scores a detected state or gesture Signal processed channels in microvolts a filtered signal Vector up to 32 numbers, tagged with a kind band powers, EMG envelopes, a feature set Your own up to 96 bytes in a layout you define anything else

The contract carries a version number. Each app records the version it was built against, and the board checks every app before starting it. An app built for an incompatible version is refused and named, both in the board's log and in what it reports to the PC. The other apps keep running.

docs.title: When an app falls behind
docs.text:
Samples wait for an app in a buffer of 256 samples. If an app falls further behind than that, it loses its oldest samples, and the loss is counted against that app alone. The recording and every other app carry on untouched.

That buffer gives each app a deadline, set by the sample rate:

Sample rate How far an app may fall behind 250 samples/s 1.02 s 500 samples/s 512 ms 1000 samples/s 256 ms 2000 samples/s 128 ms

EMG is usually recorded at the higher rates, so an EMG app has less slack than an EEG app at 250 samples/s. The board's health reports show dropped and missed samples at all times, so you can check that an app has not disturbed the recording: if those counters stay at zero while it runs, it did not.

docs.title: Controlling the board
docs.text:
Everything about how the board runs, from the sample rate to what it streams, is a setting you change from the ν-Φ app on your PC, without rebuilding anything.

  • The board decides. The PC asks for a change. The board checks the whole resulting configuration, applies it or refuses it with a reason, and reports what it is now actually doing. The PC always shows the board's report, never its own guess.
  • Presets live on the board. A role such as Participant or Noise floor is one command, and the board expands it the same way for every client.
  • Big changes need the cable. Settings that restart the board can be made only over USB, so nothing that interrupts a recording can happen over the air.
  • Settings are recorded with the data. Every recording saves the board's settings and firmware identity, with a new entry whenever a setting changes, so you can always tell how a file was recorded.

docs.title: Why it is built this way
docs.text: In research recordings the expensive failure is quiet: data that looks fine but isn't. ν-Φ is designed so that problems are loud instead. A slow app loses its own samples and says so. A mismatched app is refused by name. And the board identifies its firmware to the PC, so every file can be traced to the build that made it.

docs.title: Available now
docs.text:
• 32-channel EEG and EMG recording at 250, 500 and 1000 samples/s, controlled entirely from the PC.
  • Testing without electrodes: DAC input, internal test signals, and data streamed from the PC.
  • Preset roles, validated settings, and settings recorded with every run.
  • Apps on the board, with a versioned contract that refuses mismatched apps by name.
  • Processed signal and features at 250 samples/s.
  • Edge ML: trained models running on the board.
  • Firmware identity reported to the PC and saved with the data.

docs.title: Coming next
docs.text:
• The ν-Φ SDK. The board's acquisition half shipped as a fixed, prebuilt component, so app developers build against a stable board they never need to modify.
  • One-file desktop app. ν-Φ Studio as a single program, with the firmware image and a one-click flashing tool.
  • Processing at every sample rate. Filters and features at 500, 1000 and 2000 samples/s, which EMG work in particular needs.
  • Tablet app. Running sessions from a tablet.

docs.title: Later
docs.text: • Apps that build on other apps' results on the board, so a signal-processing app and a classifier can be written separately and composed.

docs.title: What you can do with ν-Φ
Record EEG and EMG
docs.text:
Connect surface electrodes and record EEG or EMG on up to 32 channels. Stream the raw signal to your PC at 250, 500 or 1000 samples per second, over Wi-Fi or USB. Each run gets its own folder, with the data, the board's health, and a record of every setting in force while it was made.

EEG and EMG use the same front end. What changes between them is the gain, the sample rate and the electrode montage, and all of those are set from the PC.

docs.title: Test with known signals
docs.text:
You don't need a participant to check the board or your processing.

  • From a DAC or signal generator. Drive the analog inputs with a signal you know and check the whole chain, from amplifier to result.
  • From the board's own test modes. A built-in test square checks the chain and its microvolt scaling; shorting the inputs inside the converters measures the board's own noise.
  • From the PC. Stream recorded or synthetic data straight into the board's processing, with no electrodes connected. This is how you develop an algorithm, or measure a model's accuracy on a known dataset.

docs.title: Run a ready-made mode
docs.text:
The board has preset roles, each a complete configuration chosen with one click:

Role What it does Participant a real recording: live electrodes, processed signal and features streamed Validation live electrodes, raw data only, exactly as the converters produced it Noise floor inputs shorted inside the converters, to measure the board's own noise Signal test a built-in test signal of known size, to check the whole chain and its scaling Pipeline test canned data replayed through the processing, with no electrodes Stream validate the PC sends data to the board and gets its predictions back, for accuracy testing

Change any setting by hand and the board moves to Custom, keeping exactly what you set.

docs.title: Process signals on the board
docs.text:
Filtering, notch, DC removal, envelopes and band power run on the board in real time, next to acquisition. The reference app streams a filtered signal (2–28 Hz with a 50 Hz notch) and features such as alpha power and SSVEP responses, updated ten times a second. Processed streams are available at 250 samples per second today.

For EMG, the same mechanism carries whatever your app computes, such as envelopes or RMS per channel.

docs.title: Close the loop
docs.text: Features computed on the board reach the PC with low delay, and the ν-Φ server can pass them straight to a game or display, for neurofeedback and biofeedback experiments.

docs.title: Run models at the edge
docs.text: Trained models run on the board itself and send their classifications to the PC with the data. An EEGNet model ported to ν-Φ reproduced its reference implementation's accuracy, at 74.97 % per segment and 88.12 % per trial on the project's evaluation data.

docs.title: Build your own app
docs.text: If you write processing code, you can run it on the board as a ν-Φ app, in C/C++. You get every sample from all 32 channels, the live sample rate and gain, your own memory and task, and four ways to report results. Test it on simulated data from the PC before it ever sees a participant, then run it on live signals without changing the recording side. The developer documentation covers the whole path, from the template to reading your results on the PC. Request developer access.
